one_line_contribution: It tests whether procedural agentic-memory's measured gain over a hand-written prompt survives once the comparison instruction is itself optimized (GEPA) on the exact same training episodes that built the memory bank, and separately predicts that a frozen, once-compiled instruction with no retrieval at inference (arm C / I0×M2) can match per-instance top-k retrieval (I0×M1) at matched injected tokens.
closest_prior_work: MemDelta (arXiv 2606.29914) is the real threat: it already establishes that agent-memory headline gains are artifacts of uncontrolled baselines (Mem0's 72.7-vs-61.4 win over verbatim RAG flips to a 1.2-point loss under a matched embedding model), which is the same genus of claim as this proposal's framing. It stops short of the specific mechanism, though: it never proposes a prompt optimizer as the rival container, never equalizes training episodes across containers, and never predicts that retrieval can be deleted in favor of a frozen compiled instruction. That last piece — prediction 3, the compiled-static-arm parity claim — is the part with no real precedent in the cited literature and is where this proposal's actual novelty lives; the broader 'memory-vs-optimized-instruction' framing itself is closer to prior art, since the track brief's own preamble already flags that combined memory+optimizer papers exist and fail to isolate components.
strongest_objection: Both headline predictions are load-bearing on a single model, Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, and the only cross-scale check (Llama-3.1-8B 'moderation') covers just 4 of the 7 E1 grid cells (1,2,5,6) with no positive control (B-dup) and no M2/compiled arm at 8B. That means prediction 3 — the riskier, more consequential claim that a frozen compiled instruction can replace retrieval entirely — is never tested at any scale other than the one load-bearing model. If Qwen-14B's GEPA-optimized instructions happen to absorb bank content unusually well (a property that could be an artifact of this specific model/scale rather than a general fact about instruction optimization), the paper's central practical recommendation ('compile once, delete retrieval') would not transfer to the 7B or 32B models the track's own resource brief says practitioners actually run, and a reviewer would withhold acceptance pending at least one more full-grid model.
what_would_fix_it: Run the full 7-cell E1 grid plus the B-dup positive control on at least one additional open-weight scale (e.g., 7B and/or 32B, both already in the track's stated 7B-32B range) rather than a 4-cell moderation subset, so S and the compiled-instruction parity claim are each independently tested at more than one model scale before being reported as general findings. Separately, pre-register or otherwise bound the bank-enrichment stopping rule in the precheck gate: as written, a bank that fails the +10pt gate gets iteratively enriched until it passes, which risks selecting specifically for the kind of 'instruction-shaped' memory gains GEPA is best at reabsorbing, mechanically inflating S independent of the true phenomenon.
missing_baseline: A fine-tuning/LoRA arm on the same training split. The proposal's own Related Work explicitly frames memory, instruction, and fine-tuning as the field's three candidate 'containers' for training-episode information (noting ExpeL-class papers are sometimes evaluated 'against fine-tuning'), yet the 7-cell grid tests only two of those three containers (instruction I1 vs. memory M1/M2/M3). A LoRA-tuned arm on Qwen2.5-14B trained on the identical episodes is feasible within the stated 4xA100 / open-weight-model scope and is the baseline a reviewer would demand to complete the container argument — without it the paper can only claim instruction optimization substitutes for memory, not that it is the best or cheapest substitute among the containers the field actually uses.
preprint_collision: The check is unusually rigorous and self-correcting: it explicitly retracts five citations from an earlier draft it says it 'cannot verify' (ActMem 2603.00026, MAS-PromptBench 2606.23664, TERMS-Bench 2605.13909, MemAPO 2603.21520, 'Evaluating Memory Structure in LLM Agents' 2602.11243) and refuses to lean on them for novelty — good hygiene, and better than most proposals' collision checks. But that retraction is itself a yellow flag, since it means a prior version of the novelty claim rested partly on citations that may not exist, and the current text still spends a paragraph hypothesizing about what would follow 'if TERMS-Bench exists as described,' i.e. partially re-admitting an unverified pointer into the argument. The one collision it verifies and stands behind, MemDelta (arXiv 2606.29914), is real on genus (confounded memory baselines) but not on the specific claim (rival-container substitution plus compile-don't-retrieve), so on the paper's own honestly-reported evidence there is no confirmed scooping preprint — but the check also admits it 'could not sweep OpenReview 2026 submissions,' so novelty here is asserted and reasonably supported, not fully established.
